sources.citation: Ringel, Christina. 2023. Rangga ngenandayin, lingbe berranben-nging-ngerri - Possession in Miriwoong, a non-Pama-Nyungan language of north-west Australia. PhD dissertation, Universitaet zu Koeln. KUPS 71327.
sources.note: No stress statement for either language: the Jarragan phonology remarks (sec. 2.2.1, after McGregor 2004:90-91) cover the four-vowel system and non-distinctive vowel length; the Miriwoong sketch (sec. 4.1, after Olawsky in prep. 2020) is segmental only. sources.citation: Glottolog 5.x languoid record gadj1243 and reference list (Capell 1940; ISO CR 2019-006; Bowern 2011 list; UNESCO Atlas; Ethnologue; Austlang; Barker 2004).
sources.note: No grammar, sketch or phonology reference listed (n descriptive refs = 0); Glottolog comment: Capell 1940 contains the only published Gadjerong vocabulary.

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur & Howard H. J. Coate. 1984. Comparative studies in Northern Kimberley languages. Pacific Linguistics C-69. Canberra: Department of Linguistics, Research School of Pacific Studies, Australian National University. xv+278 pp.
sources.note: Nothing for Gadjerong/Gajirrabeng or any Jarrakan language; stress remarks are about Worrorran languages only.

sources.citation: Capell, Arthur. 1940. The classification of languages in north and north-west Australia. Oceania 10(3):241-272; 10(4):404-433.
sources.note: Only an areal remark covering all north/north-west Australian languages surveyed: 'Accent is also important, though it is difficult to set down rules for it.' Gadjerong appears only in a few example words/sentences (interdental stop, verb forms); no language-specific stress statement.

sources.citation: Kaberry, Phyllis M. 1937. Notes on the languages of East Kimberley, north-west Australia. Oceania 8(1): 90-103.
sources.note: Areal remark for the languages she sampled, p. ~96: 'Stress generally falls on the first syllable, except where it contains an enclitic -- as in balo-eli: (galah -- Nyigina), or a short vowel as . (Djaru), or yu'u:ru (cloud -- Punaba).' Not about Gajirrabeng (none found for this languoid).

sources.citation: Mirima Dawang Woorlab-gerring Language and Culture Centre website (mirima.org.au: home, resources, learning-resources, site search 'Gajirrabeng').
sources.note: No Gajirrabeng dictionary, grammar or learner's guide offered publicly; only Miriwoong materials listed.

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. 2019. Change Request 2019-006 [gdh] Gadjerawang -> Gajirrabeng (submitted by Frances Kofod, supported by Knut Olawsky). SIL International.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Useful as a bibliographic pointer: cites 'Gajirrabeng-English Dictionary with English finder list and summary of grammar, Frances Kofod with Keeley Palmer and Gajirrabeng elders, Mirima Dawang Woorlab-gerring, Kununurra WA (ms for distribution to community members only) 2007' and states Kofod has recorded the language since 1971.

sources.citation: The Rosetta Project. 2010. Gadjerawang Swadesh List [16 items, phonetic transcription; forms correspond to Capell 1940]. Internet Archive item rosettaproject_gdh_swadesh-1.
sources.note: Wordlist-only: 16 words with vowel length and consonant diacritics, no stress/pitch marks, no prose.

sources.citation: McConvell, Patrick. 2009. 'Where the spear sticks up': the variety of locatives in placenames in the Victoria River District, Northern Territory. In Harold Koch & Luise Hercus (eds), Aboriginal Placenames: Naming and re-naming the Australian landscape (Aboriginal History Monograph 19), 359-402. Canberra: ANU E Press.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or tone for Jarragan. Only grammatical content: 'All the Jarragan languages appear to have a strong tendency to mark placenames with a locative suffix.. In the northern Jarragan languages.. the locative suffix following a vowel is -m with allomorphs -me, -mi, -be following consonants.' The book's other stress sentences (a full-text search for stress/accent) belong to chapters on south-eastern languages.

sources.citation: Harvey, Mark. 2008. Proto Mirndi: a discontinuous language family in northern Australia (Pacific Linguistics 593). Canberra: Pacific Linguistics.
sources.note: Nothing on Gajirrabeng prosody. The 'stress shift' remarks located by the Google Books snippet (p. 103 and sec. on subsection terms) concern Mirndi/Warlpiri/Warumungu subsection terminologies ('closed systems, are likely to be affected by lenition, shortening, stress shift and vowel harmony').

sources.citation: Moseley, Christopher (ed.). 2007. Encyclopedia of the World's Endangered Languages. London/New York: Routledge. [Wurm, Stephen A., 'Australasia and the Pacific', pp. 425-577: alphabetical language entries]
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: entry gives location, classification, speaker numbers (perhaps 3 in 1981) and 'For structural information see the Jawoyn entry'; the Jawoyn entry (p. ~503) describes only verb prefixing and noun classes, no prosody

sources.citation: Wikipedia, 'Gajirrawoong language' (cites Austlang K37.1, McGregor 2004, ABS census, WOLD).
sources.note: No phonology section; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Harvey, Mark. 2003. Reconstruction of pronominals among the non-Pama-Nyungan languages. In Nicholas Evans (ed.), The Non-Pama-Nyungan languages of northern Australia (Pacific Linguistics 552), 475-513. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics.
sources.note: No Gajirrabeng-specific prosodic statement. The stress discussion (pp. 481-483) is generic: 'In Warray, all disyllabic words are stressed on the first syllable..'; '(8) Prefixes only bear primary word stress if the verb is monosyllabic..'; the reconstructed number prefix *rrV- 'would frequently immediately precede the primary word stress, given that verb forms are commonly stressed on their first syllable' -- a cross-nPN generalisation used to explain vowel loss, with Gajirrabeng rr- merely listed among reflexes in (9). Not usable as a statement about Gajirrabeng stress.

sources.citation: McConvell, Patrick. 2003. Headward migration: a Kimberley counter-example. In Nicholas Evans (ed.), The Non-Pama-Nyungan languages of northern Australia: comparative studies of the continent's most linguistically complex region (Pacific Linguistics 552), 75-92. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics.
sources.note: Nothing. Content on Kajirrawung is morphological: pronominal enclitics vs prefixes, locative/instrumental case clitics ('In Kajirrawung, the form of the instrumental function is covered by..'; 'In Miriwung, as in Kajirrawung and unlike in Kija, Locative clitics other than neuter..'). a full-text search for stress/accent/prosod/intonation over the full text: only a generic line on clitic placement 'determined by constituent or prosodic boundaries' (p. 76, typological background).

sources.citation: McGregor, William. 1988. Handbook of Kimberley Languages, Volume 1: General information. Pacific Linguistics C-105. Canberra: ANU. Section 3.6 'Gajirrawoong / Gadjerong', pp. 45-46.
sources.note: Nothing. Bibliographic handbook entry only: '6 Word lists: Capell (1940)', '7 Textual material: None published', '8 Grammar or sketch grammar: None, but Kofod is in the process of preparing a sketch grammar.'

sources.citation: O'Grady, Geoffrey N., C. F. Voegelin & F. M. Voegelin. 1966. Languages of the World: Indo-Pacific Fascicle Six. Anthropological Linguistics 8(2): 1-197 (section 'Djeragan (XXV)', p. 78; family list p. 35).
sources.note: No phonology: states only that the five Djeragan languages (incl. Gadjerong) mark nouns for masc sg / fem sg / plural, verbs and pronouns distinguish four numbers, three persons, inclusive/exclusive, gender; verbs mark present, past, future, irrealis, imperative. Nothing on stress or tone.
